Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN)  -- North Korea qualified for the 2010 World Cup finals for the first time since 1966 by battling to a 0-0 draw away to Saudi Arabia on Wednesday night. North Korea have qualified for the World Cup for the first time since 1966. The point captured in searing temperatures in Riyadh, saw the Koreans edge into second place in Asian qualifying Group 2 to finish ahead of Saudi Arabia on goal difference and seal their place in the finals. It means both group winners South Korea, who co-hosted the World Cup with Japan in 2002, and neighbors North Korea will  play in the 2010 showpiece in South Africa. North Korea coach Kim Yong-Jun Kim had nothing but praise for his players after the final whistle. "We focused on the defending as we had come under a lot of pressure from the Saudis and I think our preparation for the game was one factor that earned the victory tonight," the North Korean boss told FIFA's official Web site. "We monitored the Saudi team from the beginning of our campaign and I noticed that they have a problem in finding good strikers. We battled to qualify for the  World Cup finals and I would like to thank my players for the great performance that they showed during the whole match," added Kim. "It was so hot in Saudi Arabia and as you know the journey from Korea was long but our belief in the ability of the players snatched the ticket to South Africa," Kim stated. The booking of North Korea's ticket to the finale will see the reclusive nation compete against the world's best despite growing international political concern regarding Pyongyang's testing of a nuclear bomb recently. Their form in the tournament is one of upsetting the odds after they Italy 43 years ago en route to the quarter-finals. The home draw sees Saudi Arabia finish in third place to go into the playoffs where they will face Bahrain. The winners will play New Zealand for a place in the finals, while Iran miss out after finishing fourth in Group 2. Earlier on Wednesday, they were denied a victory in Seoul as Manchester United midfielder Park Ji-Sung scored a late equalizer to give South Korea a 1-1 draw. Iran took the lead from an own goal early in the second half against the group winners, but Park popped up to score a brilliant 81st minute goal as he beat several men before firing home. In Group 1, Tim Cahill scored twice as Australia came from behind to beat Japan 2-1 to clinch top spot in the section. The result was academic as both teams had already sealed automatic qualification for the World Cup finals in South Africa. Japan went ahead in front of a big crowd of nearly 70,000 at the Melbourne Cricket Ground (MCG) as Marcus Tulio Tanaka headed home a Kengo Nakamura corner in the 40th minute. But the Socceroos, who went through qualifying unbeaten, hit back in the second half. Everton's attacking midfielder Cahill again worked his scoring magic to secure the victory. He was on target in the 59th and 76th minutes to take his tally to 16 in 33 internationals. "This is a step forward for us, it's great to finish top of the group," Cahill told FIFA.com after the win, while captain Lucas Neill paid tribute to their opponents. "They really played the game with intensity and they were running us ragged for a bit and we couldn't get ourselves in the game," Neill said. Bahrain later clinched third spot in the group and their playoff spot with a 1-0 win over Uzbekistan. A 74th minute goal from Mahmood Abdulrahman from a free kick gave his side a crucial three points.

# North Korea end 44-year wait to reach the World Cup

North Korea returned to football’s biggest stage for the first time since 1966 after surviving a tense final night of Asian qualifying in Riyadh.

A 0-0 draw with Saudi Arabia on 17 June 2009 secured the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea the second automatic qualifying place in AFC Group B. The result left the two sides level on 12 points, but North Korea advanced because of their superior goal difference, joining group winners South Korea at the 2010 World Cup in South Africa.

It was only North Korea’s second World Cup qualification. Their previous appearance, in England in 1966, produced one of the competition’s great surprises: a 1-0 victory over Italy and a run to the quarter-finals, where they led Portugal 3-0 before losing 5-3.

## Holding firm in Riyadh

North Korea entered their final qualifier knowing that avoiding defeat would be enough to finish above Saudi Arabia. The hosts, backed by a large crowd at King Fahd International Stadium, needed a victory to claim the automatic place.

Saudi Arabia controlled much of the possession and repeatedly pressed North Korea’s compact defensive block. Goalkeeper Ri Myong-guk and the defenders in front of him resisted the pressure, however, preserving the goalless scoreline through an increasingly anxious second half.

The visitors’ task became even harder in stoppage time when midfielder **Kim Yong-jun** was sent off. North Korea nevertheless survived the final moments and celebrated at the whistle.

The qualification campaign had been built on precisely that kind of resilience. Coach **Kim Jong-hun** organised his team around defensive discipline, collective running and swift counterattacks. North Korea conceded only five goals in eight matches during the final qualifying round and kept clean sheets in both fixtures against Saudi Arabia.

“I am very happy that we have qualified for the World Cup after 44 years,” Kim Jong-hun was quoted as saying after the decisive draw. He credited the achievement to the players’ unity and their ability to follow the team’s tactical plan under intense pressure.

Kim also acknowledged the historical importance of returning to the tournament, saying the team wanted to represent its country well in South Africa rather than be satisfied simply with qualifying.

> **Clarification:** Kim Yong-jun was a North Korean midfielder, not the national-team coach. The coach during the successful qualifying campaign was Kim Jong-hun. Kim Yong-jun was the player dismissed late in the match in Riyadh.

## A campaign based on narrow margins

North Korea’s route through the final round was rarely spectacular, but it was highly effective. They collected 12 points from eight matches, with three victories, three draws and two defeats.

Their key results included victories over the United Arab Emirates and Iran, as well as the two goalless draws against Saudi Arabia. A 1-0 win over the UAE in Pyongyang in March 2009 was particularly important, while a 2-0 home victory against the same opponents earlier in the campaign gave North Korea an early platform.

The team’s only defeats came against South Korea and Iran. Even then, North Korea remained close enough to their rivals to keep qualification in their own hands going into the last fixture.

The final Group B table was:

1. **South Korea — 16 points**  
2. **North Korea — 12 points**  
3. **Saudi Arabia — 12 points**  
4. **Iran — 11 points**  
5. **United Arab Emirates — 1 point**

North Korea’s superior goal difference separated them from Saudi Arabia and made the stalemate in Riyadh sufficient.

Qualification also meant that North and South Korea would appear at the same World Cup for the first time. South Korea had already secured first place in the group before drawing 1-1 with Iran in Seoul on the final day.

## Saudi Arabia drop into the AFC playoff

Although Saudi Arabia missed out on automatic qualification, their World Cup hopes remained alive. By finishing third in Group B, they advanced to the Asian Football Confederation playoff against **Bahrain**, the third-placed side in Group A.

Australia and Japan had taken Group A’s two automatic berths, leaving Bahrain to enter the regional playoff for the second consecutive World Cup cycle.

Saudi Arabia and Bahrain were scheduled to meet over two legs in September 2009. The winner would not qualify directly for South Africa; instead, it would advance to an intercontinental playoff against **New Zealand**, the winner of the Oceania qualifying competition.

The route therefore stood as follows:

- **AFC playoff:** Bahrain vs Saudi Arabia  
- **Intercontinental playoff:** AFC playoff winner vs New Zealand  
- **Prize:** A place at the 2010 World Cup

Bahrain eventually prevailed over Saudi Arabia on away goals after a dramatic 2-2 second leg in Riyadh, but later lost the intercontinental playoff to New Zealand.

For North Korea, no further playoff was necessary. Their disciplined draw in Saudi Arabia had completed a 44-year journey back to the World Cup—a return founded less on attacking flair than on organisation, endurance and the ability to protect the narrowest of margins.
